prompt:
You are a careful equity research analyst. Assess the competitive advantages (economic moat) and pricing power of the publicly listed company "ASML HOLDING NV" (ticker ASML), and list its competitors. Use the most recent information you know. Never invent figures: use null when unsure. Be specific (products, numbers, years).

Reply with ONLY one JSON object, no other text, in exactly this shape:
{
 "name": "official company name", "ticker": "ASML", "industry": "industry in a few words",
 "markets": ["the main product markets it competes in"],
 "mission": {"statement": "the company's own official mission statement, word for word as it publishes it; null if you are not sure of the exact wording (never paraphrase here)",
             "source": "where it is published, e.g. company website or 2025 annual report, or null",
             "plain": "what the mission means, in one short simple sentence"},
 "about": {"plain": "3-4 short sentences explaining what the company does, in simple everyday words a 12-year-old would understand; no jargon",
           "customers": "who buys from it, in one simple sentence",
           "everyday": "one sentence linking it to something ordinary people know or use, or null",
           "money": [ {"part": "business line in simple words", "share": decimal share of sales or null, "plain": "what it sells there, in a few simple words", "tag": "main|new|moonshot"} ]  (its main ways of making money, largest first, up to 6; also include any new business line or one with explosive, moonshot potential even if its sales are still small. tag: "main" = an established line that brings in a large part of sales; "new" = launched or entered in roughly the last 3 years; "moonshot" = could grow many times over or reshape the company, e.g. a new technology or market, even if unproven. Give each line one tag, the one that fits best)},
 "summary": "2-3 plain-English sentences on whether and why it has a competitive advantage",
 "pricingPower": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "specific evidence, e.g. price rises and what happened to volumes"},
 "moats": [ {"source": one of ["Brand and intangible assets","Switching costs","Network effects","Cost advantage and scale","Efficient scale","Counter-positioning","Process power (hard-to-copy know-how)","Cornered resource (exclusive asset or talent)"], "strength": "strong|moderate|weak|none", "evidence": "one or two specific sentences"} ]  (all 8 sources, in that order),
 "customers": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "customer satisfaction and loyalty: retention, NPS, reviews, repeat purchase"},
 "talent": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "ability to attract and keep top talent: employer rankings, reputation, pay"},
 "product": {"rating": "strong|moderate|weak", "evidence": "is the product best in class? independent benchmarks, awards, ecosystem"},
 "competitors": [ {"name": "company name", "ticker": "main listing ticker (exchange suffix if not US, e.g. 005930.KS) or null if private",
                   "usTicker": "ticker of its US listing or ADR that files reports with the SEC, or null", "overlap": "high|medium|low",
                   "note": "where they compete"} ]  (every significant competitor, most direct first, up to 15; include major private ones with ticker null),
 "estimates": [ {"name": "company name", "fy": "FY2025", "currency": "USD", "revenueUSDm": number, "revenueGrowth3y": decimal, "grossMargin": decimal, "operatingMargin": decimal, "netMargin": decimal} ]
   (approximate latest fiscal-year figures for the company itself and for every listed competitor; decimals, e.g. 0.42; null if unknown),
 "marketShare": [ {"market": "market name", "measure": "revenue|units|shipments|...", "latestYear": "2025", "earlierYear": "2020",
                   "rows": [ {"name": "company name", "latest": decimal or null, "earlier": decimal or null} ] } ]  (up to 3 of its main markets, the company and its main rivals),
 "threats": ["specific things that could weaken its advantage"],
 "ceo": {"name": "current CEO", "founder": true or false, "since": "YYYY", "background": "e.g. electrical engineer, Stanford MBA"},
 "checklist": { "<id>": {"verdict": "yes|partly|no|unknown", "evidence": "one specific sentence with names, numbers or examples"} }  for EVERY id below:
   "c1": Rule Breaker #1: is it the leader of an important industry that is still emerging and growing fast?
   "c2": Rule Breaker #2: why do customers choose it over rivals (brand, better value, innovation, culture, leadership), and is that advantage hard to copy and likely to last many years?
   "c3": Rule Breaker #5: do ordinary people recognise the name, is it the default leader in its field (like Google, Amazon, NVIDIA, Tesla, Intuitive Surgical, Netflix), and would customers recommend its product?
   "c4": Does it have an inspiring mission it keeps emphasising, with management driven by purpose rather than money? If it spends 10 years doing this, would it matter?
   "c6": What is the general public consensus about the company and its products or services? When people hear the name, what are the first few descriptive words that come to mind? Start the evidence with those words in quotes (e.g. “innovative, premium, reliable”), then say whether that impression is mostly positive.
   "c7": Is its total addressable market large and growing, riding a secular trend (like CRWD, NVDA, TSLA, AMZN)?
   "c8": Does it have room to expand into big new markets: in its name, its technology or its vision?
   "m1": Is the CEO a visionary with a clear picture of the future?
   "m2": Is the CEO a founder (or acting like one): long-term thinking, working extraordinarily hard, pouring heart and soul into building something that outlives them?
   "m4": Does the CEO lead by serving employees and customers?
   "m5": Has the CEO deliberately built a strong, distinctive culture that keeps inventing new products and technologies?
   "m6": Is the CEO deeply hands-on with the product and technology, ideally with an engineering background?
   "m7": Is the CEO a person of great character who cares about something bigger than profit? For successor CEOs: is stewardship aimed at the benefit of humanity?
   "m7b": Has the CEO been invited to give a commencement speech at a top university (Stanford, Harvard, MIT, etc.)? Name it.
   "m8b": Does the CEO have a distinctive, memorable personality (like Elon Musk, Alex Karp, Larry Page)?
   "m9": Has the CEO a strong record of execution and results?
   "m10": Is the CEO and company known for frugality (like Bezos's door desk)?
   "c10": Do its products solve problems for people all over the world, greatly improving the lives of a very large number of people (like NFLX, GOOG, ISRG)?
   "p2": Is what it builds extremely hard to do, and important to the world?
   "f1": Has revenue grown in almost every one of the last five years?
   "f2": Have gross and operating margins risen over the last five years?
   "f3": Is debt low compared with cash and cash flow, with positive shareholders' equity?
   "f4": Have operating income and operating cash flow risen over the last five years?
   "v1": Is its main product clearly the best in its field, with a practical reason an ordinary person can understand for choosing it over every alternative (like NVIDIA over AMD)?
   "v2": Is it widely seen as one of the best companies to work for (culture, mission, reputation, employer rankings)? Cite rankings.
   "c5": Do its products make the world better? If it disappeared overnight, who would notice and miss it, and why?
 "asOf": "YYYY-MM of the newest information you used"
}

result.name: ASML Holding N.V.
markets: DUV lithography systems (ArF immersion, ArF dry, KrF, i-line)

mission.statement: Together with our partners, we provide leading patterning solutions that drive the advancement of microchips.
mission.source: ASML company website (About ASML: vision and mission)
mission.plain: ASML builds the machines that print ever-smaller patterns on chips so chips keep getting better.

about.plain: ASML is a Dutch company that builds giant, very precise machines that print tiny circuit patterns onto silicon wafers using light. These patterns become the chips inside phones, computers and AI servers. Its newest machines use extreme ultraviolet light and are so hard to build that no other company in the world makes them. It also services and upgrades the thousands of machines already in chip factories.
about.customers: Chipmakers such as TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK hynix and Micron buy its machines.
about.everyday: Almost every advanced chip in your smartphone or in the servers behind ChatGPT was patterned on an ASML machine.

money.plain: older-style deep-ultraviolet lithography and measuring tools
extreme-ultraviolet machines for the most advanced chips (48% of 2025 system sales)
servicing, upgrades and spare parts for installed machines
next-generation EXE machines that print even finer patterns
research on even higher-resolution EUV for chips in the 2030s

result.summary: ASML has one of the strongest moats in any industry: it is the only company that makes EUV lithography machines, which every leading-edge chip (from TSMC, Samsung, Intel) depends on. Its advantage rests on decades of R&D (€4.7B in 2025), an exclusive supply chain with partners such as Zeiss, and a huge installed base it services, though it is exposed to chip cycles and export controls.

pricingPower.evidence: Total net sales rose 15.6% to €32,667M in 2025 while gross margin increased from 51.3% to 52.8%, reached 54.0% in Q2 2026 with 2026 guidance of 54-56%, and ASML targets 56-60% by 2030 as each EUV generation sells at higher prices.

moats.evidence: ASML's thousands of lithography patents and its reputation as the indispensable supplier of EUV make it the default choice of every leading-edge chipmaker.
Chipmakers design processes, masks and fabs around ASML tools for years, and its installed-base business (€8,193M in 2025, up 26.2%) ties customers to ASML service and upgrades.
There are no direct user network effects, although the shared ecosystem of mask, resist and design-tool makers built around ASML's platforms reinforces its position.
With €32.7B of 2025 sales ASML can spend €4.7B a year on R&D, more than Nikon's and Canon's lithography sales combined, and spread EUV development costs over 48 EUV systems recognised in 2025.
The market for leading-edge lithography is too small and too costly to support a second EUV supplier; Nikon and Canon dropped out of EUV development.
ASML's early bet on outsourcing modules to partners and co-funding by customers (Intel, TSMC, Samsung invested in 2012) helped it overtake Nikon, but this is now history rather than a current edge.

EUV took about two decades to commercialise and requires integrating tin-plasma light sources (a 1,000-watt source was demonstrated in April 2025) and near-perfect optics, know-how rivals have not replicated.
Carl Zeiss SMT supplies EUV optics exclusively to ASML (ASML owns 24.9% of it), and ASML employs more than 16,000 R&D staff with an attrition rate of 4.1% in 2025.

customers.evidence: ASML's customer satisfaction survey score was 88% in 2025 (86% in 2024), and net bookings rose to €28,035M in 2025 from €18,899M, with a year-end backlog of €38,797M.

talent.evidence: ASML has more than 44,000 employees, including more than 16,000 in R&D, with low attrition of 4.1% in 2025, and is one of the most sought-after technology employers in the Netherlands.

product.evidence: Its NXE EUV scanners are the only tools able to print the most advanced chip layers, and its EXE High-NA systems (four revenue systems recognised in 2025) extend that lead.

competitors.name: Nikon Corporation
competitors.note: Makes ArF immersion, ArF dry and KrF DUV lithography scanners; no EUV.

competitors.name: Canon Inc.
competitors.note: Makes KrF and i-line steppers and nanoimprint lithography (FPA-1200NZ2C) as an alternative patterning method.

competitors.name: Shanghai Micro Electronics Equipment (SMEE)
competitors.note: Private Chinese lithography maker developing domestic DUV scanners with state support.

competitors.name: SiCarrier (Huawei-linked) and other Chinese EUV efforts
competitors.note: Private Chinese efforts to build domestic lithography, including EUV prototypes, to replace ASML under export controls.

competitors.name: KLA Corporation
competitors.note: Competes with ASML's YieldStar and HMI metrology and inspection tools.

competitors.name: Applied Materials, Inc.
competitors.note: Competes for chipmakers' equipment budgets and in e-beam metrology and patterning alternatives (e.g. Centura Sculpta).

competitors.name: Lam Research Corporation
competitors.note: Competes for chipmakers' equipment budgets; etch and deposition can reduce or add patterning steps.

competitors.name: Tokyo Electron Limited
competitors.note: Makes the coater/developer tracks paired with ASML scanners and competes for wafer-fab equipment budgets.

threats: US and Dutch export controls limiting sales of EUV and advanced DUV immersion tools to China, which fell from 41% of system sales in 2024 to 33% in 2025.
Customer concentration in a few chipmakers (TSMC, Samsung, Intel, SK hynix, Micron) whose capital spending is cyclical.
Slower-than-hoped adoption of High-NA EUV if customers keep using multi-patterning with low-NA tools.
Chinese state-backed efforts (SMEE, Huawei-linked SiCarrier) to build domestic lithography, which could shrink its China business.
Alternative patterning approaches such as Canon's nanoimprint lithography and advanced etch/deposition reducing lithography intensity.
Tariffs and geopolitical tensions disrupting its global supply chain of about 5,100 suppliers.

ceo.name: Christophe Fouquet
ceo.background: French physicist-engineer who worked at KLA and Applied Materials before joining ASML in 2008, where he led the EUV business.

c1.evidence: ASML is the sole supplier of EUV lithography, the key enabler of leading-edge and AI chips, and expects 2026 sales of €43-45B, up from €32.7B in 2025.

c2.evidence: Customers have no alternative for EUV, and its exclusive Zeiss optics partnership and decades of know-how make the advantage very hard to copy.

c3.evidence: ASML is the undisputed default leader in lithography and customers rate it 88% in satisfaction surveys, but few ordinary consumers know the name.

c4.evidence: Its purpose, 'Unlocking the potential of people and society by pushing technology to new limits', is emphasised consistently, and its work underpins continued progress in computing.

c6.evidence: “monopoly, high-tech, indispensable”; the impression is overwhelmingly positive, though it is often mentioned in news about US-China chip export controls.

c7.evidence: ASML cites a semiconductor industry projected to surpass $1 trillion in sales by 2030, driven by AI, and sees €44-60B of annual revenue by 2030.

c8.evidence: It can grow with High-NA EUV, metrology and services, but it remains focused on lithography for chips rather than entering new industries.

m1.evidence: Fouquet has set out a clear roadmap of High-NA and future Hyper-NA EUV and capacity expansions (about 65 low-NA EUV systems for 2026, plus 30% for 2027).

m2.evidence: Fouquet is a long-time insider (since 2008) who led the EUV business and thinks long term, but he is a professional manager rather than a founder.

m4.evidence: ASML stresses collaboration with customers and suppliers and its 'We care' value, but there is little specific public evidence of Fouquet's personal servant-leadership style.

m5.evidence: ASML's culture of 'We challenge, we collaborate, we care' has repeatedly delivered breakthrough products, from EUV to High-NA and a 1,000-watt EUV source in 2025.

m6.evidence: Fouquet is a physics-trained engineer who ran ASML's EUV business before becoming CEO.

m7.evidence: Under Fouquet ASML emphasises enabling technology for humanity's challenges, but there is no unusual public evidence of personal causes beyond the business.

m7b.evidence: No record found of Fouquet giving a commencement speech at a top university.

m8b.evidence: Fouquet is a low-profile technical executive with no celebrity-style public persona.

m9.evidence: Since he became CEO in April 2024, sales rose to a record €32.7B in 2025 and 2026 guidance was raised to €43-45B with gross margin of 54-56%.

m10.evidence: ASML is not publicly known for frugality, and it invests heavily in R&D (€4.7B in 2025).

c10.evidence: Nearly every advanced chip in phones, PCs, cars and AI data centres worldwide depends on ASML's lithography machines.

p2.evidence: EUV machines took about two decades to develop and are among the most complex machines ever built, yet they are essential to the world's chip supply.

f2.evidence: Gross margin was 52.7% in 2021 and 52.8% in 2025 and operating margin 35.1% versus 34.6%, roughly flat, though Q2 2026 gross margin rose to 54.0%.

f3.evidence: At end-2025 ASML held €13,322M of cash and short-term investments and generated €12,659M of operating cash flow, against modest bond debt and shareholders' equity of €19.6B.

f4.evidence: Operating income rose from €6,536M (2021) to €11,301M (2025) but dipped in 2022 (€6,501M) and 2024 (€9,023M), and operating cash flow rose from €11,166M in 2024 to €12,659M in 2025.

v1.evidence: For EUV there is no alternative at all: a chipmaker that wants to make the most advanced chips must buy ASML's machines.

v2.evidence: ASML is a highly attractive employer for engineers in the Netherlands with 4.1% attrition in 2025, but it is not a fixture of global best-workplace rankings.

c5.evidence: If ASML disappeared, progress in advanced chips for AI, phones and computers would stall, which every chipmaker and tech company would notice immediately.
